652.title: Stand the night
652.hook: O you wrapped in garments, stand in the night, except a little (73:1–2)
652.howItsDone: Many Muslims pray tahajjud, voluntary night prayer in units of two rak'ahs, after sleeping and before dawn; some keep it nightly, many especially in Ramadan, following the call of al-Muzzammil and the Prophet's practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mosques are for Allah, and your line, the mosque is his. Did an ordinary spot look like a place of prayer? Today, a new surah, and a call that comes in the dark. Day six hundred fifty-two.

It's the middle of the night. The house is asleep. You're under a heavy blanket, pulled up to your chin, the warmest you've been all day. And someone speaks to you, gently, by the name of what you're doing. You, wrapped up. Get up. Not all night. Most of it, or half, or a little less. That is how surah seventy-three begins. It's addressed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and it calls him by his blanket: al-muzzammil, the one wrapped up.

Verses one and two, in Pickthall's translation: "O thou wrapped up in thy raiment! Keep vigil the night long, save a little." Then verses three and four make it flexible: half the night, or a little less, or a little more. Many commentators hear the name as tender: not a formal title but a description, almost a nickname. They note that Arabs sometimes addressed someone by what they were doing at that moment, as a kind of affection. Many scholars connect the wrapping to the beginning of revelation. Sahih al-Bukhari tells how, after the first revelation in the cave of Hira, the Prophet came home shaking and said to his wife Khadijah: wrap me, wrap me. Commentators differ on whether this surah came right after that, but it is counted among the early ones. And then the call: stand. Qiyam al-layl, standing the night in prayer. Verse six explains why: rising by night is stronger for the heart and more fitting for words. The night is quieter. Nobody's watching. Your phone, ideally, is face down. Whatever you say in prayer at two in the morning, you mean. Verse five gives another reason: We are about to send down on you a weighty word. Before the heavy work of carrying the message in daylight, the Prophet was given the training of the night. Today this practice has a name many Muslims know well, tahajjud, voluntary prayer after sleep, in the last part of the night. Some do it every night, some during Ramadan, some only now and then. The invitation of the surah is the same: get up from the blanket, and stand.

The practice: two units at night. If you pray, you're invited tonight, or before dawn, to get up and pray two short units, two rak'ahs, even if it's only once this week. For now, sit as if it were the middle of the night. Lower the lights if you can. Let the house go quiet in your mind. Notice how different your attention feels when nobody needs anything from you. Stay in that quiet. The bell holds the time.
Stand the night. In 73:1–2 the Prophet, wrapped in his garments, is called to rise and pray through the night, all but a little. Today's word.
Your line: stand in the night. Tonight, set an alarm a little before dawn, or simply sit up for two minutes before sleep, and spend them in quiet prayer or stillness. Day six hundred fifty-two.

653.title: Measured tones
653.hook: recite the Qur'an in slow, measured rhythm (73:4)
653.howItsDone: Muslims learn to recite the Qur'an with tartil and the rules of tajwid, often from a teacher from childhood: slow, clear, with lengthened vowels and pauses at verse ends, in prayer and in daily reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Muzzammil, and your line, stand in the night. Did you find two quiet minutes, before sleep or before dawn? Today, how to recite once you're standing. Day six hundred fifty-three.

Play a podcast at double speed and you'll get the information. You won't get the person. The pauses, the breath before a hard sentence, the way a voice slows down when it means something: all gone. Most of us now read, listen and even pray at double speed. The same verse that calls the Prophet to stand the night tells him how to recite once he's standing. And the instruction is one word, repeated twice, in a way that sounds exactly like what it asks for.

Verse four ends, in Pickthall's translation: "and chant the Qur'an in measure." The Arabic is wa rattili al-Qur'ana tartila. Rattil, and then tartil: the verb and its noun together, which in Arabic adds emphasis. Recite it in measure, truly in measure. Tartil means a recitation that is slow, clear, evenly spaced, each letter given its full sound. Classical Arabic dictionaries connect the root r-t-l with things set out neatly and evenly, like well-spaced teeth. Every sound gets its own room. How did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ actually recite? His wife Umm Salamah was asked, and according to reports in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, she described his recitation as distinct, letter by letter, pausing at the end of each verse. And Anas ibn Malik, in Sahih al-Bukhari, said he would draw out the long vowels. From verses like this one grew an entire science, tajwid, the rules for pronouncing the Qur'an correctly: where to lengthen, where to pause, how each letter is formed. Children around the world spend years learning it. Different reciting styles developed too, slower and more melodic, or plainer. But they share the measure. Why does it matter? Verse five gives a hint: We are about to send down on you a weighty word. You don't carry something heavy at a run. You carry it slowly, with your full attention. Tartil is what attention sounds like out loud. The slowness isn't a delay before the meaning. It's how the meaning gets in.

The practice: one surah, very slowly. If you know a short surah, al-Fatiha or al-Ikhlas, recite it now, in Arabic or in translation, at half your usual speed. Give every word its full sound. Pause at the end of each verse, and breathe. If you don't know one, take any line you love and say it the same way, a word at a time, as if each word were heavy. Then sit in the quiet after. The bell holds the time.
Tartil. Slow, clear, measured recitation, each letter given its room. In 73:4: rattili al-Qur'ana tartila, recite it in measure. Today's word.
Your line: slowly, measured. Today, pick one thing you'd normally rush, a prayer, a message, a sentence to someone you love, and say it at half speed. Day six hundred fifty-three.

654.title: Recite what is easy
654.hook: He knows you can't keep it all, so recite what is easy for you (73:20)
654.howItsDone: For most Muslims night prayer (tahajjud) is voluntary, and many keep a small, steady portion of it, or a daily portion of Qur'an recitation, following 73:20 and the hadith that the religion is easy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tartil, and your line, slowly, measured. Did one rushed thing get said at half speed? Today, the last verse of al-Muzzammil, and it changes the rules. Day six hundred fifty-four.

Some resolutions are too big to keep. Run every morning. Read for an hour a day. Never check the phone after nine. Two weeks in, you're exhausted, and then you quit the whole thing. Surah al-Muzzammil began with a huge ask: stand half the night in prayer, sometimes more. And the Prophet and some of those with him tried, night after night. And then the surah's last verse arrives, much longer than the others, and it says something that sounds almost like relief.

Verse twenty speaks straight to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: your Lord knows that you stand nearly two thirds of the night, or half, or a third, and so do some of those with you. He knows you can't keep count of it all. So He has turned to you in mercy. Then: recite of the Qur'an what is easy for you. And it names why. Some of you will be sick. Some will be traveling the land, seeking a living. Some will be fighting in the cause of Allah. So recite what is easy of it. The verse knows people's lives. Illness, work trips, hard duties. It doesn't pretend they don't exist. A hadith in Sahih Muslim, from 'A'ishah, gives the history. When the surah began, she said, night prayer was made obligatory, and the Prophet and his companions kept it for a year. Allah held back the end of the surah for twelve months, then revealed this lightening, and the night prayer became voluntary. Notice what didn't change. The verse doesn't say: forget it. It says: recite what is easy. The practice stays; its size changes. And it adds the things that keep going no matter what: establish the prayer, give the zakat, lend Allah a good loan, ask His forgiveness. Muslims often quote a hadith from Sahih al-Bukhari alongside this verse: the religion is easy, and whoever makes it too hard will be overcome by it. The surah doesn't lower the bar to zero. It sets it where a real person can keep stepping over it.
screen: `HE KNOWS YOU CAN'T KEEP IT ALL.`

segments.voice: The practice: do what's easy, but do it. Sit, and think of one good habit you dropped because it got too big. Prayer, reading, exercise, calling your mother. Now shrink it until it's easy. One verse instead of a page. One minute instead of thirty. One call a week. Make it small enough that you'd be embarrassed not to do it. Then decide when you'll do it today. The bell holds the time.
Recite what is easy. In 73:20 the night vigil is lightened: Allah knows you'll be sick, traveling and striving, so recite what is easy. Today's word.
Your line: what is easy. Today, do the small version of the habit you picked, the easy one, and actually do it. Day six hundred fifty-four.

655.title: Arise and warn
655.hook: O you cloaked, arise, magnify your Lord, purify your garments (74:1–4)
655.howItsDone: Muslims pray in clean clothes on a clean place, and many read 74:4 as calling for purity of both garments and heart; the surah is remembered as the call that began the Prophet's public mission.

segments.voice: Yesterday: recite what is easy, and your line, what is easy. Did the small version of your habit actually happen? Today another surah that begins with someone covered up, and a call to get up. Day six hundred fifty-five.

After the first revelation in the cave, the tradition says, the visits stopped for a while. Days, maybe longer. Then one day, walking, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ heard a voice and looked up. The same angel he'd seen in the cave was there, filling the space between sky and earth. He ran home shaking and said to his family: cover me, cover me. They wrapped him in a cloak. And under the cloak, the next words came. Surah seventy-four, al-Muddaththir, the one cloaked.

The surah opens, in Pickthall's translation: "O thou enveloped in thy cloak, Arise and warn! Thy Lord magnify, Thy raiment purify." The story of the cloak is in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah. Jabir even thought this surah was the very first revelation; most scholars say al-'Alaq came first, and al-Muddaththir came soon after the pause. Either way, these are the words that turned a private experience into a public mission. Look at the four commands. Qum: arise. Get out from under the cloak. Fa-andhir: and warn. Tell people what's coming. Wa rabbaka fa-kabbir: and your Lord, magnify. The same root as Allahu akbar, God is greater. Before you warn anyone, set Allah above everything, including your own fear. And thiyabaka fa-tahhir: your garments, purify. Here the commentators split. Some read it literally: keep your clothes clean, especially for prayer. Others read garments as a picture of the self: purify your deeds, your heart, your intentions. Many hold that both meanings are meant, the outer and the inner together. Then verse five adds: and shun what is foul. Notice the order. Get up. Speak. Make Allah great in your eyes. Clean yourself, inside and out. It's a morning routine for someone about to face a hostile city. The Prophet had just said cover me. The answer was: arise. Not a rebuke. A job, and the dignity that comes with being given one.

The practice: a clean garment. For now, sit up straight and notice what you're wearing. Smooth a sleeve, straighten a collar, brush something off your knee. Do it slowly, with care, as if getting ready for something important. Then, inside, do the same: notice one thing in your heart you'd like to wash out today, a grudge, a lie, a bad mood. Later today, if you can, wash and iron one garment and put it aside for prayer or for a good day. The bell holds the time.
Arise and warn. In 74:1–4 the Prophet, wrapped in a cloak, is told: arise, warn, magnify your Lord, purify your garments. Today's word.
Your line: arise. Today, when you want to pull the covers over something you have to do, take one breath and get up for it. Day six hundred fifty-five.

656.title: Don't give to get more
656.hook: do not give expecting to get more (74:6)
656.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to give charity without reminding the recipient of it or expecting return, citing 74:6 and 2:264; many give secretly so that, as a hadith says, the left hand doesn't know what the right gave.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arise and warn, and your line, arise. Did you get up for something you wanted to hide from? Two verses further into al-Muddaththir, a fifth command. Day six hundred fifty-six.

You know the gift with a string on it. The favor that comes back up in an argument six months later: after everything I did for you. The wedding present chosen to impress. The donation made mostly for the plaque. The help offered so that, one day, help will be owed. Most giving has a little ledger behind it, even when we don't admit it. Just after the call to arise, al-Muddaththir gives the Prophet a short instruction that goes straight at that ledger.

Verse six is four words in Arabic: wa la tamnun tastakthir. Don't give, seeking more. Tamnun comes from mann, which carries two ideas: to bestow a favor, and to remind someone of it, to hold it over them. Tastakthir means to seek more, or to count something as a lot. And the commentators read the verse in more than one way. One early reading, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, is the plainest: don't give a gift so that you'll get a bigger one back. Another reading: don't consider what you've done as much. Don't stand before your Lord counting your good deeds as if they were a favor to Him. A third: don't remind people of the good you've done for them. Many commentators say the verse holds all of these. They're the same habit, seen from different sides: keeping score. The Qur'an returns to this in surah al-Baqarah, where it says: don't cancel your charity with reminders and hurt. A gift held over someone isn't really a gift anymore; it's a loan with interest. And look at what comes right after, verse seven: for your Lord, be patient. The giving and the patience are a pair. If you give without expecting a return, you'll need patience, because sometimes nothing comes back. No thanks, no favor, no recognition. The verse doesn't promise you'll be repaid by people. It removes the repayment from the transaction entirely. You give, and then you let it go, and you wait, if you wait at all, on Someone else.

The practice: give with nothing in return. Sit, and think of someone you could give something to today. Time, a meal, a ride, a coin, a kind word. Then check for a string. Do I want thanks? Credit? A favor later? Don't scold yourself if you find one; almost everyone does. Just notice it, and picture cutting it. Picture giving, and then not mentioning it to anyone, ever. The bell holds the time.
Don't give to get more. In 74:6, wa la tamnun tastakthir: don't give seeking more, don't count your good as much, don't hold it over anyone. Today's word.

657.title: The self that blames itself
657.howItsDone: Many Muslims practice muhasabah, taking oneself to account, often at night, reviewing the day's words and deeds; teachers describe the self in three states drawn from the Qur'an: urging to wrong, self-blaming, and at peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday: don't give to get more, and your line, give, don't count. Did a gift go out with no string on it, and stay out of the conversation? Today a new surah, al-Qiyamah, and an oath by something inside you. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

You said something sharp at dinner. Everyone moved on. But at eleven at night, brushing your teeth, a small voice starts up: that wasn't fair. You should apologize. Why did you say that? Nobody else heard it. Nobody else needed to. That voice, the one that won't let you off the hook, is so ordinary that most people never think about it. The Qur'an does. At the start of surah seventy-five, it swears by it, right next to the Day of Resurrection.

Surah al-Qiyamah opens with two oaths. Verse one: I swear by the Day of Resurrection. Verse two, in Pickthall's translation: "Nay, I swear by the accusing soul (that this Scripture is true)." The Arabic is an-nafs al-lawwamah. Nafs is the self, the soul, the inner person. Lawwamah is an intensive form from lawm, blame: the self that blames, and keeps blaming, again and again. Why put it next to the Day of Resurrection? Commentators have suggested that the conscience is a small preview of that day. A reckoning that happens inside you, every evening, long before the final one. Muslim writers later drew a map of the self from three Qur'anic phrases. An-nafs al-ammarah, in surah Yusuf: the self that urges toward wrong. An-nafs al-lawwamah, here: the self that blames itself afterward. And an-nafs al-mutma'innah, in surah al-Fajr: the self at peace, called home to its Lord. Many teachers describe these as stages, or as three voices everyone hears at different times. Al-Hasan al-Basri, an early scholar of Basra, is reported to have said that a believer is always taking himself to account, while a careless person moves ahead without looking back. Notice what the blaming self is not. It isn't despair, and it isn't self-hatred. In the map, it's a good sign, a step up from the self that only urges. It's the part of you that still cares about the truth. The verse honors it with an oath. The aim is to listen to it, make things right, and move toward the peace after it.

The practice: notice your conscience. Sit, and walk back through the last day. Wait for the place where the small voice speaks up: that wasn't fair, that wasn't true, that wasn't kind. Don't argue with it, and don't pile on. Just hear what it's actually saying. Then ask it one question: what would make this right? Let the answer be small and doable. The bell holds the time.
The self that blames itself. An-nafs al-lawwamah, the conscience that keeps calling you back, honored with an oath in 75:2. Today's word.

658.title: Don't hurry your tongue
658.hook: don't move your tongue to hurry the revelation; its collecting is on Us (75:16–17)
658.howItsDone: Muslims learning the Qur'an are taught to listen to a teacher's recitation first and then repeat it, a method that echoes 75:16–19 and Ibn 'Abbas's account of how the Prophet received revelation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the self that blames itself, and your line, the voice that blames. Did you listen to it, and do the small thing it asked? Today, the same surah, and a moment in the middle of revelation itself. Day six hundred fifty-eight, the end of a week.

Have you ever tried to take notes while someone was talking too fast? You scribble, you whisper the words to yourself, you fall behind, and you lose the next sentence because you were still holding the last one. Now imagine the words are from God, and you're terrified of losing even one. In surah al-Qiyamah, in the middle of verses about the Last Day, the Qur'an suddenly turns and speaks to the Prophet about exactly that: his lips, moving too fast.

Verses sixteen and seventeen, in Pickthall's translation: "Stir not thy tongue herewith to hasten it. Lo! upon Us (resteth) the putting together thereof and the reading thereof." The story behind it is in the first pages of Sahih al-Bukhari. Ibn 'Abbas explained that when revelation came, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ found it heavy, and he would move his lips, repeating the words as they came, for fear of forgetting them. And then Ibn 'Abbas did something lovely: he moved his own lips, to show his student how the Prophet had done it. His student, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, did the same for the next generation. A gesture handed down like a family recipe. Then these verses came. Don't rush. Collecting it in your heart, and its recitation, are Our responsibility. Verse eighteen: when We recite it, follow its recitation. Verse nineteen: then its explanation is on Us too. After this, Ibn 'Abbas said, when Jibril came, the Prophet would listen. And when Jibril left, he would recite it as it had been recited to him. Notice the shape of it. First listen. Then speak. The memory wasn't his burden to carry by force. It would be given. Surah Ta Ha has a similar line: don't be in haste with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say, my Lord, increase me in knowledge. There's something here for anyone who learns anything. The fear of forgetting can make you grab so hard that you stop listening. The verse says: let go of the grabbing, and listen all the way to the end.
screen: `STIR NOT THY TONGUE TO HASTEN IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: slow your recitation. If you know a short surah or prayer, don't say it yet. First, listen to it in your mind, all the way through, without moving your lips. Then, when it's finished, recite it once, slowly, the way it came to you. If you don't know one, do the same with any line you love. Listen first. Speak second. Notice how different it feels to not be chasing the words. The bell holds the time.
Don't hurry your tongue. In 75:16–17 the Prophet is told not to rush the revelation: its gathering and recitation are on Allah. First listen, then recite. Today's word.

Your line: don't hurry. This week ran from stand in the night, slowly measured, what is easy, arise, give don't count, and the voice that blames, to here. Today, in one conversation, let the other person finish completely before you speak. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

Ibn 'Abbas says so, in Sahih al-Bukhari.
after these verses, he recited along with Jibril word for word
he listened, and recited after Jibril left.
verse nineteen says the explanation is also on Allah
gathering, recitation and explanation: all on Us.

fork.setup: you're the Prophet. revelation is coming, heavy and fast, and you fear you'll forget a word. what do these verses tell you?
options: repeat each word as it comes.
listen to the end; its gathering is on Us.
fork.reveal: don't hurry your tongue. listen, follow the recitation, and its collecting and explanation are on Allah.

original.note: Arabic, 75:16: don't move your tongue with it (to hurry it).

trapdoor: what you thought: speak slowly.
what it means: the Prophet was told to stop rushing the words of revelation; listening first, the memory would be given.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari's fifth hadith preserves Ibn 'Abbas moving his lips, shown to his student; 75:16–19 assigns gathering, recitation and explanation to Allah.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5 (Ibn 'Abbas on the Prophet moving his lips)
